transcript:
Meeting header: 2025-02-12 15:00 UTC | Duration: 62 mins | Attendees: Samira Khan (Redwood AE), Luis Ortega (Redwood SE), Maya Patel (Redwood SRE), Daniel Reed (CTO, HyperDoc), Priya Nair (ML Eng), Alex Wu (Infra), Jordan Lee (Product)

00:00 Speaker 1 (Samira): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick intros then we will dive into the long-context perf questions around your 128k use cases.
00:18 Speaker 2 (Daniel): Thanks Samira. We have pretty heavy docs, legal and engineering archives, need to run QA and search across 100k+ token contexts.
00:28 Speaker 1 (Samira): Got it. Luis, can you lead on the runtime/tech details?
00:33 Speaker 3 (Luis): Sure. The core problems for 128k+ are memory, kv cache growth, attention compute, and how chunking interacts with batching. I'm going to walk through strategies we use.
00:45 Speaker 4 (Priya): Quick note — for our workflows we do retrieval-augmented generation, so we often bring in 50-200 chunks per session and then do QA.
00:55 Speaker 3 (Luis): Perfect. So first, chunking: you can do fixed-size chunks with overlap, or semantic chunking. For 128k context we usually recommend chunk sizes of 4k-16k tokens with overlap of 10-20% depending on coherence needs. Overlap increases KV cache re-use but costs more tokens.
01:15 Speaker 3 (Luis): Example: 128k divided into 16k windows equals 8 chunks; with 10% overlap it's ~9-10 windows worth of compute. We precompute embeddings and retrieval vectors so you only stream in top-k chunks to the model.
01:32 Speaker 5 (Alex): Is there a hard limit? We heard some models drop off after 64k.
01:37 Speaker 3 (Luis): Model architecture and tokenizer matter. Some open models we've validated can be extended to 128k using attention modifications. For very long sequences we apply attention optimizations.
01:47 Speaker 3 (Luis): Sliding window attention: you only attend to a local neighborhood for most layers and use global attention for the retrieved chunk or the query tokens. This reduces quadratic cost to linear-ish per layer for long sequences. It has tradeoffs in cross-chunk reasoning.
02:05 Speaker 3 (Luis): Sparse attention or block-sparse kernels (e.g., sparse combos, BigBird-like patterns) are another option; they let you keep global tokens and connect blocks probabilistically. Both approaches are effective but require model support or custom kernels in the runtime.
02:20 Speaker 4 (Priya): How does KV cache scaling work in Redwood's runtime? We need low latency when a user scrolls across a long doc and asks follow-ups.
02:30 Speaker 6 (Maya): Our runtime streams KV pages and supports prefix/KV caching beyond single request. For 128k it's impractical to recompute all past KV for each query; we keep a summarized prefix and warm the KV pages on demand.
02:44 Speaker 6 (Maya): Two operational patterns: ephemeral KV per session (fast, no persistence), or persisted KV (checkpointed to disk or object store). Persisted KV lets you resume sessions without recompute, but you need storage and network I/O considerations.
02:58 Speaker 5 (Alex): For on-prem, we'd prefer local NVMe-backed caching to avoid egress. Does Redwood support that?
03:04 Speaker 6 (Maya): Yes, for Private/on-prem we support local NVMe cache for KV shards and allow HSM/KMS integrations for keys. We'll provide config templates.
03:12 Speaker 2 (Daniel): Latency is critical. We target interactive p95 under 2s for follow-ups. What kind of numbers can we expect?
03:22 Speaker 3 (Luis): It depends on the model size, quantization, and chunk count. Ballpark: with a 70B-ish model quantized to 4-bit and optimized kernels, steady-state tokens/sec for generation can be 1.5k-3k tokens/sec on a single A100-like GPU for short contexts. For 128k-like contexts, initial retrieval and KV warming add overhead — first response could be 5-12s depending on how many chunks need warming. Subsequent follow-ups that hit the warmed KV can be sub-2s.
03:52 Speaker 4 (Priya): Do you have example p99s?
03:55 Speaker 3 (Luis): p99 is highly workload-dependent. If you need worst-case guarantees we recommend Dedicated reserved capacity so we can tune batching and memory. In our tests with a 70B variant and sliding-window attention, p99 for a 1-2k token answer with warmed KV was ~2.8s; cold start with 128k recompute could hit ~12-18s.
04:17 Speaker 5 (Alex): That's a lot. Any ways to reduce cold-start?
04:20 Speaker 6 (Maya): Pre-warming: run a lightweight pass that computes KV for top-n chunks ahead of time; prefetch most-likely chunks based on retrieval scores. Also you can persist KV between sessions for known documents.
04:33 Speaker 3 (Luis): Another trick is progressive decoding and streaming answers while backfilling context — you can start generating from the retrieved highest-confidence chunks and expand as more KV is loaded. That gives perceived latency improvements.
04:47 Speaker 2 (Daniel): What about batching? Our app has many concurrent users; we need high throughput but also predictable latency for interactive sessions.
04:55 Speaker 3 (Luis): Continuous batching helps — route similar latency-sensitive requests to low-latency pools and batch at small window sizes (e.g., 8-16) to avoid adding too much batching latency. For throughput-heavy offline jobs, you can batch larger. Redwood Dedicated supports configurable batch size windows per pool.
05:13 Speaker 5 (Alex): Any guidance on batch size vs p99?
05:16 Speaker 3 (Luis): Larger batch sizes increase throughput but add wait time. If your target p95 is <2s, we recommend small batch windows (<20ms hold) and using dedicated pools. We can surface token-level cost tradeoffs in the spreadsheet.
05:27 Speaker 4 (Priya): Let's talk quantization. We need to understand quality regressions for 4-bit.
05:33 Speaker 3 (Luis): Quantization (4-bit, 6-bit, 8-bit) reduces memory and improves throughput but can impact output quality. For many models, 4-bit carefully calibrated (GPTQ or AWQ) yields near-parity on standard benchmarks; but on nuanced legal language you may see subtle degradation. We recommend a hybrid approach: quantize most weights to 4-bit but keep critical layers (e.g., first/last layers, attention) in higher precision or use quantization-aware finetuning for sensitive workloads.
05:59 Speaker 2 (Daniel): Are quantized models compatible with the KV cache approach?
06:04 Speaker 3 (Luis): Yes. Runtime supports quantized kernels and a quantized KV layout. The KV memory footprint drops substantially, which helps scale to 128k. But we must test for hallucination/regression risks on your prompt sets.
06:16 Speaker 5 (Alex): On network security: if we do Private VPC, what's the peering and egress model?
06:22 Speaker 6 (Maya): We support VPC peering and private link. For on-prem, we can run the full control plane in your VPC with no egress, or a customer-managed control plane and isolated inference plane. We'll share SOC2 and network diagrams.
06:36 Speaker 4 (Priya): Any constraints around KMS/HSM?
06:39 Speaker 6 (Maya): We integrate with customer KMS via standard APIs; for air-gapped deployments we can support on-prem HSMs. Keys never leave the customer's environment in Private mode.
06:49 Speaker 2 (Daniel): Can Redwood run model variants with custom attention kernels on our infra? We run some experimental sparse-attention patches.
06:55 Speaker 3 (Luis): We can onboard custom kernels but it adds engineering time. For Dedicated and Private we can build and certify kernels against the runtime. For open-source sparse-attention variants, we typically evaluate feasibility and then integrate if it proves stable.
07:08 Speaker 5 (Alex): How do you measure token throughput for long contexts?
07:12 Speaker 3 (Luis): We measure end-to-end tokens/sec including retrieval, KV loading, and generation. For long-context sessions the metric of interest is tail latency per query and tokens/sec over a session. We also instrument KV page fault rates and cache hit ratios.
07:26 Speaker 4 (Priya): If we have multimodal docs (images + text) chunking feels harder. Any recommendations?
07:32 Speaker 3 (Luis): Combine multimodal chunks into a joint embedding and treat each as a retrieval unit; keep chunk sizes consistent across modalities and tune overlap based on semantic boundaries. The runtime supports multimodal prefixes but the main perf constraints still come from tokenized text length.
07:46 Speaker 2 (Daniel): Ok, let's get into some concrete numbers. Could we run a pilot: 10 sessions, each with 128k initial context and 4 follow-ups, and measure p50/p95/p99 and cost?
07:58 Speaker 1 (Samira): Yes, that's exactly what we can run. Luis, Maya — plan?
08:03 Speaker 3 (Luis): We'll create a benchmark harness to run 10 parallel sessions, using progressively warmed KV strategies and compare approaches: full recompute, persisted KV, pre-warm top-k, and sliding-window kernels. We'll report p50/p95/p99, tokens/sec, GPU memory utilization, and cost estimates.
08:17 Speaker 6 (Maya): On infra we'll test two profiles: Dedicated cloud GPU (A100/NVIDIA H100) with 4-bit quantization, and on-prem reference with NVMe-backed KV shards. We'll record page fault rates and prefetch latency.
08:31 Speaker 5 (Alex): If we do on-prem, do we get the same telemetry and console?
08:35 Speaker 6 (Maya): Yes, we provide private console access and local agents that push metrics to your preferred observability backends. We can also emit traces for per-token latency.
08:46 Speaker 4 (Priya): Any gotchas with tokenization and chunk boundaries causing information loss?
08:51 Speaker 3 (Luis): Yes, naive chunking can split entities. Use semantic chunk boundaries (sentence/paragraph) and token-aware alignment. Also overlap helps preserve context for tokens at edges. We'll share a chunking library we use for stable boundaries.
09:04 Speaker 2 (Daniel): How much room for improvement is there on attention optimizations?
09:08 Speaker 3 (Luis): A lot. We've seen 2-4x speedups in long-context workloads by moving from dense attention to a hybrid sliding+global model with optimized kernels and fused rotary ops. Kernel-level fusion (qk, softmax) and using memory-efficient attention (flash attention variants) also yields significant reductions in memory and time.
09:28 Speaker 5 (Alex): Flash attention combined with chunk streaming — are there memory alignment challenges?
09:33 Speaker 3 (Luis): Yes, you need strong kernel implementations and contiguous KV layout. On GPUs you also watch out for PCIe vs NVLink bandwidth when streaming KV from CPU memory. That's why NVMe-local and GPU-local storage reduce variance.
09:48 Speaker 6 (Maya): For on-prem installs we'll recommend NVLink-enabled nodes and provisioning for peak KV working set. We can produce sizing guidance based on your corpus size.
10:00 Speaker 4 (Priya): Regarding quality, will quantization plus sparse attention produce weird edge-case hallucinations?
10:06 Speaker 3 (Luis): Potentially. That's why we do evals over targeted seed prompts. We run quality checks and regression tests tied to prompt sets. Redwood Optimize can recommend maintaining higher precision for critical layers.
10:18 Speaker 5 (Alex): Are there any licensing issues with using patched kernels?
10:21 Speaker 3 (Luis): Depends on the kernel license. For in-house patches we can run them in Private, but Redwood's hosted catalog uses certified kernels. We'll make sure to review OSS licenses.
10:31 Speaker 2 (Daniel): What's the timeline to get a pilot? We want to be ready for a Q2 feature launch.
10:36 Speaker 1 (Samira): If we start the pilot this month we can aim for a 4-week pilot and have data for a Q2 decision. Luis, can you estimate engineering time?
10:45 Speaker 3 (Luis): For a standard harness and one model variant, 7-10 business days to set up benchmarks and configs. If we need custom kernel onboarding for on-prem, add 2-4 weeks.
10:54 Speaker 4 (Priya): Are there cost estimates for Dedicated vs Private on-prem?
10:58 Speaker 1 (Samira): We'll include rough cost models in the benchmark sheet — per token plus reserved capacity numbers for Dedicated. For Private we'll provide a licensing + infra sizing estimate.
11:08 Speaker 5 (Alex): Anything else on compliance? We need SOC2, ISO, and detailed audit logs for queries.
11:12 Speaker 6 (Maya): We provide audit logs and token-level traces, and can increase retention for compliance packages. We'll send the SOC2 report and an architecture appendix for our Private offering.
11:21 Speaker 2 (Daniel): Sounds good. Can you also show end-to-end trace examples so our infra team can understand network hops?
11:26 Speaker 6 (Maya): Yes, will include sample traces and latency waterfall charts.
11:31 Speaker 1 (Samira): Recap: Redwood will share benchmark spreadsheet and configs, run a 10-session pilot using your sample docs, and schedule an on-prem POC if results look good. HyperDoc will provide sample documents and network topology. Action items noted.
11:44 Speaker 2 (Daniel): Thanks everyone. We'll follow up via email and update the CRM.
11:49 Speaker 1 (Samira): Thanks, meeting adjourned.

Notes on transcript quality: automated transcription had a few mis-attributed lines and occasional tokenization errors around model names. The tech content above includes noisy speech (ums/ahs) that were lightly cleaned for readability.
